concept.name: Granger causality
concept.definition: A statistical precedence concept: a series x Granger-causes y if past values of x improve the forecast of y beyond what past values of y alone provide, tested by F-tests on lagged coefficients in an autoregression or VAR. Introduced by Granger (1969).
concept.intuition: If knowing yesterday's thunder helps predict today's rain beyond what yesterday's rain tells you, thunder Granger-causes rain: it is incremental predictive content, not metaphysical cause.
concept.mechanics: Regress y_t on p of its own lags (restricted model), then add p lags of x_t (unrestricted model); an F-test of the joint null that all x-lag coefficients are zero rejects Granger non-causality. The test runs in both directions and generalizes in a VAR to block-exogeneity Wald tests.
concept.formula: In y_t = a_0 + sum_{i=1}^p a_i y_{t-i} + sum_{j=1}^p b_j x_{t-j} + e_t, x Granger-causes y if the b_j are jointly non-zero (F-test of H_0: b_1 = ... = b_p = 0).
concept.failure_modes: Results are sensitive to lag length, sample period, and omitted variables: an omitted common driver manufactures apparent causality. With integrated or cointegrated data, standard F-test distributions are invalid without Toda-Yamamoto or VECM adjustments.
concept.misconceptions: That Granger causality is true causality: it is only incremental predictability within the chosen information set, and enlarging that set can reverse the conclusion.
concept.example: Testing whether money-supply growth Granger-causes GDP growth amounts to adding lagged money growth to an autoregression of GDP growth and jointly testing its coefficients.
